stories.headline: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.title: Unleashing India's potential over 25 years
stories.summary: On October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi took oath as chief minister of Gujarat. Twenty-five years later, that milestone offers an opportunity to reflect not only on a quarter century of public service, but also on how profoundly India itself has changed during the same period.I have had the privilege of witnessing this transformation through the lens of business. The Mahindra Group has businesses across 20 industries that comprise nearly 70 percent of India’s GDP, including agriculture, mobility, technology, financial services, aerospace, logistics, real estate and hospitality. Across these sectors, one change has been unmistakable: The scale of the India opportunity has expanded dramatically.In 2001, India had enormous potential, but that potential was constrained by gaps in infrastructure, connectivity, technology and access. Today, India is a far more connected, capable and globally consequential economy.The numbers tell part of the story. India’s economy was around $500 billion in 2001; by 2026, it is close to $4 trillion. But GDP alone cannot capture the transformation. The more interesting story is how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more.Connectivity to opportunityConsider how an Indian citizen interacts with the economy today.A small entrepreneur can receive a payment instantly from a customer thousands of kilometres away. A farmer can access information through a mobile phone. A young person in a small town can build a business for a global market. A consumer can access financial services without necessarily stepping into a bank branch.Digital public infrastructure has changed the architecture of opportunity. Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and UPI have helped deepen financial inclusion and formalisation, while UPI has demonstrated how technology, scale and inclusion can work together.This is not simply a technology story. It is an India story: The movement from access being a privilege to access becoming increasingly ubiquitous.Also Read: 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi in public office: Shaping governanceFrom infrastructure deficit to a new realityThe physical transformation has been equally significant.India has expanded its highways, airports, ports, metro systems, rail networks and digital connectivity at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago. We are adding an airport a month for the past few years, and more than 30 to 34 km of roads daily, nearly three times the pace a decade ago. Electricity access, too, has expanded dramatically, with World Bank data showing 99.5 percent access in 2023.Infrastructure is not an end in itself. It is an enabler. Better connectivity allows a manufacturer to source more efficiently, a farmer to reach markets faster, a tourist to travel more easily and a young person to access opportunities beyond the geography in which they were born.What I saw from the industry sideMy year as President of FICCI gave me another perspective on this transformation.We worked with more than 500 CEOs and 30 ministries on more than 100 initiatives spanning Make in India, women-led development, farm prosperity and sustainability. I personally participated in more than 200 meetings with senior government leaders and saw first-hand how industry and government could engage on complex economic and policy questions.What stayed with me was the willingness to listen.Industry would bring specific recommendations, sometimes involving difficult policy choices. The response was often to engage with the substance: To ask questions,challenge assumptions and explore what could be done.Constructive dialogue matters. Government brings the policy framework and public-interest perspective; industry brings ground-level experience, investment and execution capability. When the two engage seriously, the potential for outcomes that benefit both the economy and businesses increases.I believe this partnership will be particularly important in India’s next phase of growth.Potential to executionPerhaps the most important change has been India’s growing confidence in executing at scale.Over the past decade, the country has undertaken large national programmes across financial inclusion, sanitation, housing, renewable energy, digital infrastructure and manufacturing. The pandemic provided a particularly powerful demonstration of India’s ability to coordinate institutions, technology, manufacturing and public systems at enormous scale.For business, this creates a new opportunity. India is no longer only a large market to serve. It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity. Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains. As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.But opportunity is not automatic. Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology. The aspiration should be straightforward: Make world-class products in India, innovate in India and compete with the world.The next frontier is peopleThe next 25 years will require a different kind of transformation.India’s greatest asset is its people. Our demographic dividend will become an economic dividend only if young Indians have the education, skills and opportunities required for the jobs of the future.We must focus on skilling youth for industry readiness with industry as an active participant.We must also unlock the enormous potential of women in the workforce. Greater participation is not only a question of equity; it is an economic imperative. A country of India’s scale cannot realise its full potential if a significant part of its talent remains under-utilised.Businesses, therefore, have a responsibility beyond creating jobs. We must build skills, encourage entrepreneurship and create pathways for more people to participate meaningfully in the formal economy.Growth must also become increasingly sustainable. Climate change, energy transition, resource security and urbanisation will shape the competitiveness of both nations and companies. Long-term value creation will need to consider financial performance alongside the impact on people, communities and the environment.From potential to prosperityPerhaps the greatest transformation is intangible.In 2001, India was often described through the lens of what it could become. Today, the conversation increasingly centres on what India can build, lead, and contribute to the world.Indian entrepreneurs are building global companies. Indian technology is reaching international markets. Indian manufacturing is becoming part of global supply chains. Indian innovations in digital payments, healthcare and space are attracting global attention.Yet confidence must be accompanied by humility. India still has significant challenges—from inequality and skills to urbanisation, agricultural productivity, and the creation of quality employment.Twenty-five years of public service, therefore, provides an opportunity not simply to look back, but to ask what comes next.The India of 2001 had aspiration. The India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability. The India of 2047 must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.That is the next chapter of the India story and one that all of us have a role in writing.

opening: On October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi took oath as chief minister of Gujarat.
Twenty-five years later, that milestone offers an opportunity to reflect not only on a quarter century of public service, but also on how profoundly India itself has changed during the same period.
body: I have had the privilege of witnessing this transformation through the lens of business.

The Mahindra Group has businesses across 20 industries that comprise nearly 70 percent of India’s GDP, including agriculture, mobility, technology, financial services, aerospace, logistics, real estate and hospitality.
Across these sectors, one change has been unmistakable: The scale of the India opportunity has expanded dramatically.
In 2001, India had enormous potential, but that potential was constrained by gaps in infrastructure, connectivity, technology and access.
Today, India is a far more connected, capable and globally consequential economy.
The numbers tell part of the story.
India’s economy was around $500 billion in 2001; by 2026, it is close to $4 trillion.
But GDP alone cannot capture the transformation.
The more interesting story is how opportunity has increasingly moved from being concentrated in a few places and institutions to becoming accessible to millions more.
Connectivity to opportunityConsider how an Indian citizen interacts with the economy today.
A small entrepreneur can receive a payment instantly from a customer thousands of kilometres away.
A farmer can access information through a mobile phone.
A young person in a small town can build a business for a global market.
A consumer can access financial services without necessarily stepping into a bank branch.
Digital public infrastructure has changed the architecture of opportunity.
Aadhaar, Jan Dhan and UPI have helped deepen financial inclusion and formalisation, while UPI has demonstrated how technology, scale and inclusion can work together.
This is not simply a technology story.
It is an India story: The movement from access being a privilege to access becoming increasingly ubiquitous.
From infrastructure deficit to a new reality.
The physical transformation has been equally significant.
India has expanded its highways, airports, ports, metro systems, rail networks and digital connectivity at a scale that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago.
We are adding an airport a month for the past few years, and more than 30 to 34 km of roads daily, nearly three times the pace a decade ago.
Electricity access, too, has expanded dramatically, with World Bank data showing 99.5 percent access in 2023.
Infrastructure is not an end in itself.
It is an enabler.

Better connectivity allows a manufacturer to source more efficiently, a farmer to reach markets faster, a tourist to travel more easily and a young person to access opportunities beyond the geography in which they were born.
What I saw from the industry sideMy year as President of FICCI gave me another perspective on this transformation.
We worked with more than 500 CEOs and 30 ministries on more than 100 initiatives spanning Make in India, women-led development, farm prosperity and sustainability.
I personally participated in more than 200 meetings with senior government leaders and saw first-hand how industry and government could engage on complex economic and policy questions.
What stayed with me was the willingness to listen.
Industry would bring specific recommendations, sometimes involving difficult policy choices.
The response was often to engage with the substance: To ask questions,challenge assumptions and explore what could be done.
Constructive dialogue matters.
Government brings the policy framework and public-interest perspective; industry brings ground-level experience, investment and execution capability.
When the two engage seriously, the potential for outcomes that benefit both the economy and businesses increases.
I believe this partnership will be particularly important in India’s next phase of growth.
Potential to executionPerhaps the most important change has been India’s growing confidence in executing at scale.
Over the past decade, the country has undertaken large national programmes across financial inclusion, sanitation, housing, renewable energy, digital infrastructure and manufacturing.
The pandemic provided a particularly powerful demonstration of India’s ability to coordinate institutions, technology, manufacturing and public systems at enormous scale.
For business, this creates a new opportunity.
India is no longer only a large market to serve.
It can increasingly be a place from which to build products, technologies and businesses for the world.
Manufacturing will be central to this next chapter.
The global reconfiguration of supply chains presents India with an important opportunity.

Initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes have sought to attract investment, deepen domestic capabilities and integrate Indian manufacturers more closely with global value chains.
As of December 2025, the schemes had attracted more than ₹2.16 lakh crore of investment and generated over ₹20 lakh crore in production and sales across 14 sectors.
But opportunity is not automatic.
Productivity, skills, logistics, ease of doing business and supply-chain competitiveness will determine how far India can go.
At the Mahindra Group, we see this every day—in automobiles, tractors, electric mobility, aerospace and advanced technology.
The aspiration should be straightforward: Make world-class products in India, innovate in India and compete with the world.
The next frontier is people.
The next 25 years will require a different kind of transformation.
India’s greatest asset is its people.
Our demographic dividend will become an economic dividend only if young Indians have the education, skills and opportunities required for the jobs of the future.
We must focus on skilling youth for industry readiness with industry as an active participant.
We must also unlock the enormous potential of women in the workforce.
Greater participation is not only a question of equity; it is an economic imperative.
A country of India’s scale cannot realise its full potential if a significant part of its talent remains under-utilised.
Businesses, therefore, have a responsibility beyond creating jobs.
We must build skills, encourage entrepreneurship and create pathways for more people to participate meaningfully in the formal economy.
Growth must also become increasingly sustainable.
Climate change, energy transition, resource security and urbanisation will shape the competitiveness of both nations and companies.
Long-term value creation will need to consider financial performance alongside the impact on people, communities and the environment.
From potential to prosperityPerhaps the greatest transformation is intangible.
In 2001, India was often described through the lens of what it could become.
Today, the conversation increasingly centres on what India can build, lead, and contribute to the world.
Indian entrepreneurs are building global companies.
Indian technology is reaching international markets.
Indian manufacturing is becoming part of global supply chains.
Indian innovations in digital payments, healthcare and space are attracting global attention.
Yet confidence must be accompanied by humility.
India still has significant challenges—from inequality and skills to urbanisation, agricultural productivity, and the creation of quality employment.
Twenty-five years of public service, therefore, provides an opportunity not simply to look back, but to ask what comes next.
The India of 2001 had aspiration.
The India of 2026 has demonstrated growing capability.
The India of 2047 must translate that capability into broad-based, sustainable and enduring prosperity.
That is the next chapter of the India story and one that all of us have a role in writing.

stories.headline: Statements, overtures & conduct of the 'regime-change gang' expose their own intent
stories.title: Statements, overtures & conduct of the 'regime-change gang' expose their own intent
stories.summary: FRAGRANCE OF IDEAS With the onset of the month of October 2026, there was once again a campaign of street protests, unauthorised gatherings disrupting the normal routine of life and social media-based noise trying to hoodwink the opinion of the general masses seen in a few cities and towns of the country. Their main focus was on the capital of the country -New Delhi. Some other cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata, Hyderabad and Chennai were also affected marginally. The main issue this time was the so-called resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gaynesh Kumar, for his organisation's nationwide work on Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls (SIR). The primary organisers this time were parties and forums like Congress, AAP and CJP. Having failed to achieve anything tangible in political terms after the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, the then Minister for HRD, in July 2026, all such elements made it sure that more and more chaos, confusion and an environment of political abuse and hatred against the people in power at the Centre and the institutions established by the Constitution and law are made as the new rules of the game. They do so to create a perpetual atmosphere of violence, law and order and anarchy throughout the length and breadth of the country, irrespective of its negative impact on the economic growth, peace, progress and the status of the country among the comity of nations. And they do it brazenly in the name of 'saving the constitution'. Earlier in the month of June and July this year, their main agenda was the paper-leak, NEET examination reforms and the resignation of the HRD Minister. The way the organisers, and mainly the newly formed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) was provided 'accommodation' by the government in regard to the holding of their protest and other allied activities surely gave the organisers a claim of victory. The 20th July unauthorised rally at and outside the Jantar-Mantar, followed by violence and arson in Delhi, brought several facts to light and gave a real and befitting introduction of the organisers -CJP to the public at large. Their real faces were unmasked consequent upon the unfortunate events of 20th July, which in a way dashed their moral standing in the eyes of the countrymen. The CJP, after the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, began a campaign of 'school reforms' and started making their trips to various government schools without any proper permission from the authorities. However, they chose to keep their campaign limited to the BJP-NDA-ruled states and didn't venture to go beyond that. Opposition-ruled states were exempted from such atrocious campaigns, which angered the people concerned. Thus, they received a lukewarm response to their campaign, and at several places, the people started to oppose their entry into their villages and surroundings. They received tough opposition even in public parks and grounds in sub-urban areas at several places. It was in the month of September, 2026 that the CJP announced to go for one more protest demonstration on 10 October, 2026 at Jantar-Mantar, New Delhi to press for the resignation of the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar. Now, they converted their movement into a full-fledged politically oriented agitation. Armed and alarmed both by their announcement, the Congress party, which believed that the resignation of the CEC was their exclusive agenda supported by a few other parties, counter-announced their own plan to organise their protests on the same issue. The Congress held its nationwide protests, with a focus in Delhi, to march towards the CEC's office on 25th September 2026 to exert pressure for the resignation of the CEC on their invented flimsy grounds. The Congress agitators faced police barricades at the BJP headquarters and the Nirvachan Sadan in Delhi. In order to build a false narrative on the issue, some other protests by opposition groups and individuals were also organised on 3 and 6 October, 2026, in which the police detained some demonstrators for protesting without permission at Jantar-Mantar. On 6 October, senior leaders of the opposition INDI alliance, including Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Akhilesh Yadav, staged a march to the Election Commission office and were blocked by police barricades near the Election Commission headquarters. The leaders, without any permission, instead gate-crashed the adjacent Akashwani Bhavan premises and again staged a two-hour sit-in protest there. Several leaders were detained and released later. The government and the administration this time took extra and exclusive measures unlike July 20, 2026 and didn't grant any permission for any sort of assembly at Jantar-Mantar. All precautions were made to maintain public order. Authorities enforced a massive security lockdown in central Delhi to foil any rally planned by the CJP. The CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and other senior organisers of CJP were detained immediately upon landing at the Delhi airport. The other passengers in the flight also rebuked the CJP leaders for their conduct. On the other hand, the police sealed off Jantar Mantar, closed 45 metro stations, cancelled incoming trains, and detained over 2,000 people to prevent any unauthorised assembly in the capital. Though there were some provocations that could escalate the situation and create violence, arson and law-and-order situations bigger than on 20 July, 2026, but the police administration remained alert and vigilant to foil all such designs. This time, only a few hundreds of people gathered on the roads surrounding Jantar-Mantar who were not allowed to enter the debarred venue. Criminals and history-sheeters were also not allowed to enter the crowd of protesters. Then people opposed to such protests and agitations also joined the crowd and raised slogans in favour of the police and the government headed by PM Narendra Modi. The regular media and the social media was also seen divided this time, putting before their respective viewpoints while covering the protests. In nutshell, the protests failed and couldn't achieve anything tangible to show. The top three detained CJP leaders were released by the magistrate only on the production of a peace-bond with the condition that they wouldn’t do anything to disturb peace and tranquillity for one year, in addition to surety. In the meantime, the statements, overtures and conduct of the leaders and the prominent activists of all these protests further clarified the intent and the ultimate motives of the organisers of all these protests. While some leaders on the front said that they stand inspired by the Bangladesh events of regime change there and would be thankful to them for showing them the way, others attacked all constitutional institutions and authorities and also talked in terms of revolution, including a bloodbath. People in general ignored the appeals and repeated requests by the organisers from Congress, AAP and CJP to reach Delhi in lakhs to join their planned activities against the CEC and the government. On 12 October 2026, Rahul Gandhi and other leaders of Congress, along with a few thousand of their activists, defied the prohibitory orders and marched towards the Supreme Court of India and tried to make the Apex Court a party to their political agitation. The Supreme Court of India last year upheld the decision of the EC to conduct SIR at the national level and also said they have the constitutional sanction to do their duties. On the issue of fresh requests from the opposition for an intervention, the CJI declined a direct meeting with the political delegation, and instead the court asked them to file their appeal with the Court for hearing. This brazen attempt to involve the Apex Court in such a political event was done for the first time in such a manner. The government on the recommendations of the committee set up earlier to the effect cancelled Jantar-Mantar for any future protests and notified three other venues for any sort of protests including the Ramlila Maidan. It was welcomed by most people as it wouldn't cause inconvenience to the general public in future. On 16 October, 2026, the CJP attempted another march at Connaught Place, New Delhi. The government took the attempt very seriously in view of the importance of Connaught Place being the centre of activity, particularly during the festive season. Security personnel locked down Central Park and enforced Section 163 of the BNSS. CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Neha Bora were taken into preventive custody prior to the event, leading to scattered flop protests and standoffs between the activists and counter-protesters who opposed any such programme in the vicinity. Dipke once again submitted another bond before the magistrate to desist from any activity for one year causing damage to peace and public order. His two other colleagues were put in the police remand for five days for breaking prohibitory orders at Jantar-Mantar by the Special Executive Magistrate. The Congress as a follow-up has asked for permission for a protest rally at Ramlila Maidan from October 25 to November 3, 2026 which the administration in Delhi has granted to them. Some other Andolan-Jeevis have also announced their march scheduled for October 23, 2026. A Sanyukt Kisan Morcha organised Delhi Chalo march is also on cards the same day. For the last 10 years, all these parties, forums and individuals who have been losing the elections consistently and continuously are having only one target in mind. That is to topple a duly elected government at the centre headed by Modi. Their frustration has led them to a situation to speak lies about the SIR conducted by the EC and have further lost their space in the minds of the people. Fake earlier narratives like 'Chowkidar chor hai', 'vote-chori', 'EVM frauds', 'vote chor-gaddi chod' etc have already drawn flak and public has not been convinced with these slogans at all excepting the usual activists of the respective parties. Rahul Gandhi's campaigns, slogans, marches, unauthorised gate-crashings and other such irresponsible behavior in public have also been a cause of bringing further disrepute to the opposition and particularly the Congress. Entry and involvement of foreign elements and funds in such protests and demonstrations against the PM, HM, CEC and the government are an open secret. Rahul Gandhi's pronouncements on different podiums that the real targets are the PM and the HM, and CEC is only a beginning are also stunning. Those who are advocating their cause have also been advocating regime change on the pattern of situations in Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, Nepal and other places where democratically elected governments were thrown through anarchy, violent unrest and foreign intervention. The government and the administration in India seem to have learnt lessons about these anarchists who are hell-bent on trampling the peace and progress of the country. What they are unable to achieve through a democratic process and constitutional means, they want to do it with unfair and unconstitutional ways on the streets and don't feel shy about the way their intent and conduct are causing damage to the country. People have seen through their motives and have also generally kept themselves aloof from such activities and useless agitations. It is time for the Congress, AAP and the INDI-alliance, and also the CJP, to introspect and have a deep evaluation of their flop shows throughout, along with the growing public anger against them. (The author is a senior BJP & KP leader, Human Rights Defender and a columnist and can be reached at: ashwanikc2012@gmail.com )

Their frustration has led them to a situation to speak lies about the SIR conducted by the EC and have further lost their space in the minds of the people.

Fake earlier narratives like 'Chowkidar chor hai', 'vote-chori', 'EVM frauds', 'vote chor-gaddi chod' etc have already drawn flak and public has not been convinced with these slogans at all excepting the usual activists of the respective parties.

Rahul Gandhi's campaigns, slogans, marches, unauthorised gate-crashings and other such irresponsible behavior in public have also been a cause of bringing further disrepute to the opposition and particularly the Congress.
Entry and involvement of foreign elements and funds in such protests and demonstrations against the PM, HM, CEC and the government are an open secret.
Rahul Gandhi's pronouncements on different podiums that the real targets are the PM and the HM, and CEC is only a beginning are also stunning.

Those who are advocating their cause have also been advocating regime change on the pattern of situations in Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bangladesh, Nepal and other places where democratically elected governments were thrown through anarchy, violent unrest and foreign intervention.
The government and the administration in India seem to have learnt lessons about these anarchists who are hell-bent on trampling the peace and progress of the country.

What they are unable to achieve through a democratic process and constitutional means, they want to do it with unfair and unconstitutional ways on the streets and don't feel shy about the way their intent and conduct are causing damage to the country.
People have seen through their motives and have also generally kept themselves aloof from such activities and useless agitations.
It is time for the Congress, AAP and the INDI-alliance, and also the CJP, to introspect and have a deep evaluation of their flop shows throughout, along with the growing public anger against them.
(The author is a senior BJP & KP leader, Human Rights Defender and a columnist and can be reached at: ashwanikc2012@gmail.com ).

In order to build a false narrative on the issue, some other protests by opposition groups and individuals were also organised on 3 and 6 October, 2026, in which the police detained some demonstrators for protesting without permission at Jantar-Mantar.

On the other hand, the police sealed off Jantar Mantar, closed 45 metro stations, cancelled incoming trains, and detained over 2,000 people to prevent any unauthorised assembly in the capital.

stories.headline: ‘Winds of change are blowing”: Dr Farooq
stories.title: ‘Winds of change are blowing”: Dr Farooq
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: National Conference president Dr Farooq Abdullah on Monday termed the Supreme Court’s 2024 verdict upholding the abrogation of Article 370 “entirely wrong”, claiming that the court had described the provision as permanent in two earlier hearings before its abrogation in August 2019. Addressing a party workers’ convention in Beerwah, he reiterated the NC’s commitment to fighting for the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status and full statehood. He said that before the abrogation of Article 370 on August 5, 2019, the Supreme Court, in two earlier hearings, had upheld the provision’s permanent status and described it as a permanent provision of the Constitution of India. He asserted that the National Conference would continue its struggle for the restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional rights and special status. Highlighting the historic contributions of the National Conference, Dr Farooq said that the party’s revolutionary and historic initiatives had paved the way for land reforms, enabling poor and marginalised farmers and cultivators to acquire ownership rights over land. He said that it was also due to the National Conference that the light of education reached every household in Jammu and Kashmir, with the literacy rate rising from 6 per cent to nearly 82 per cent today. He added that the party’s role in establishing and strengthening fundamental, constitutional and democratic institutions, as well as essential infrastructure, remained unforgettable. Dr Farooq Abdullah said that repeated attempts and conspiracies had been made over the past several decades to weaken the National Conference, but with the unwavering support of the people and the grace of Almighty Allah, the party had overcome every challenge. He asserted that as long as the people stood firmly with the National Conference, no force could undermine its political strength. Targeting the PDP, Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the hardships endured by the people of Jammu and Kashmir over the past several years were a consequence of the PDP’s actions. He said that the National Conference had announced unconditional support to the PDP in 2014 and warned it against bringing the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, cautioning that the party would wreak havoc in the region. However, he said, the PDP ignored the warning and pushed the state towards destruction. Had the PDP not brought the BJP to Jammu and Kashmir, Article 370 would not have been abrogated, he added. He described the Supreme Court’s 2024 judgment on Article 370 as entirely wrong, arguing that the same court had upheld the provision on two earlier occasions and stated that it had acquired permanent status under the Constitution of India. “Almighty Allah is watching everything. We need only to exercise patience and restraint. Oppression may last for a while, but it cannot continue forever. Allah will certainly bring oppression to an end, and injustice will be eradicated,” he said. “The winds of change have begun to blow, and they are gathering speed.” Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the people of Jammu and Kashmir were seeking their rightful due. He recalled that promises had been made regarding delimitation, elections and the restoration of statehood following the elections. “Where have those promises gone? Why has statehood still not been restored even after two years?” he asked. He said that, in January this year, National Conference Members of Parliament had met the Union Home Minister in New Delhi, where the latter had assured them that business rules would be provided immediately to clarify the respective powers of the Lieutenant Governor and the elected government. However, he said, even after ten months, the promised business rules remained nowhere in sight. He said those in power are relying on false promises and deception. Speaking about the current development scenario, Dr Farooq Abdullah said that the government led by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah was utilising all available resources to accelerate development across Jammu and Kashmir despite the most challenging circumstances. He said that every possible effort was being made to provide relief to the people. The initiation of several development projects in different parts of Jammu and Kashmir, including Beerwah constituency, reflected a new phase of progress, he added. At the conclusion of the convention, party leaders reiterated their commitment to public service, inclusive development and the protection of Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional rights. They expressed confidence that the National Conference would continue to enjoy the support of the people in the future.

stories.headline: Green Spaces Are Srinagar’s First Defence
stories.title: Green Spaces Are Srinagar’s First Defence
stories.summary: Srinagar is often described through its lakes, gardens, mountains and chinar trees. The city’s beauty is not merely ornamental; it is rooted in a fragile ecological balance that has shaped its climate, culture and public life for centuries. Yet, as Srinagar expands, its urban green spaces are steadily being reduced, fragmented or treated as leftover patches of land waiting for construction. This is not simply a loss of scenery. It is a warning about the kind of city we are building and the quality of life we are willing to accept. Urban green spaces are frequently regarded as luxuries—pleasant additions to a city that can be planned after roads, markets, buildings and parking lots have been provided. That approach is both outdated and dangerous. Parks, wetlands, gardens, open fields, tree-lined avenues and riverfront vegetation are essential components of urban infrastructure. They regulate temperature, absorb rainwater, reduce air pollution, support biodiversity and create common spaces where people can breathe, walk, meet and recover from the pressures of crowded urban life. Srinagar needs this infrastructure urgently. The city’s growth has brought new roads, commercial complexes, residential colonies and institutions. But expansion without ecological planning has placed extraordinary pressure on the land. Open spaces are shrinking, natural drainage channels are being narrowed or blocked, wetlands are being encroached upon, and mature trees are being removed in the name of development. Each individual intervention may appear small or unavoidable. Together, they are altering the city’s environmental character. The consequences are already visible. Summers feel harsher, traffic emissions remain trapped in congested areas, rainwater accumulates quickly after heavy showers, and neighbourhoods that once had open breathing spaces are becoming dense and concrete-bound. The loss of vegetation also weakens the city’s ability to withstand flooding, air pollution and rising temperatures. In a valley known for its cold winters and moderate summers, the growing heat of concrete surfaces should not be dismissed as a minor inconvenience. A city without adequate green cover becomes unhealthy in more ways than one. Children lose safe places to play. Older residents lose accessible spaces for walking and social interaction. Women and families are deprived of comfortable public areas. People living in smaller homes, especially in dense neighbourhoods, lose the opportunity to spend time outdoors without having to travel long distances. The absence of parks is therefore not only an environmental concern; it is also an issue of public health, social equity and urban dignity. Srinagar’s green spaces also carry historical and cultural meaning. The city’s gardens, avenues and tree-lined landscapes are part of its memory. The chinar is not just a tree planted for decoration; it is woven into the region’s identity. The same is true of the open spaces around water bodies, the gardens that have served generations, and the public grounds where people have gathered during different seasons. When such spaces disappear, a city loses more than trees. It loses continuity with its own past. The danger lies partly in the absence of a clear public understanding of what constitutes a green space. A park is easy to recognise, but urban ecology extends beyond formally designated gardens. A wetland on the edge of a neighbourhood, a patch of native trees, a stream corridor, a community playground, a strip of vegetation beside a road or an open field can all perform vital ecological functions. They should not be judged only by their commercial value or immediate development potential. Planning authorities must therefore move beyond the narrow idea that land is either “developed” or “vacant.” Much of what appears vacant is performing work that is invisible until it is gone. Wet ground stores excess water. Trees filter dust and provide shade. Grass and soil absorb rainfall. Vegetation around water bodies protects their banks and supports birds and other species. An open field may serve as a temporary flood buffer, a playground and a community gathering space at the same time. Once these functions are destroyed, replacing them is neither easy nor cheap. Srinagar requires a comprehensive urban green-space policy that is based on mapping, protection and public access. Every ward should have a clear inventory of its parks, playgrounds, wetlands, tree belts, water channels and open areas. These spaces must be recorded, legally protected and monitored. Their boundaries should not be altered quietly through piecemeal permissions or gradual encroachment. Equally important is the need to establish minimum green-space standards for every neighbourhood. Urban planning cannot remain focused only on floor area, road width and parking capacity. It must ask whether residents have access to trees, open ground, shaded walking routes and safe recreational spaces. New colonies and large construction projects should be required to include usable public green areas, not merely decorative lawns hidden behind walls. The quality of green space matters as much as its quantity. A neglected patch of land with broken fencing and accumulated waste cannot substitute for a functioning public park. Green spaces must be designed for people of different ages and abilities. They should have walking paths, seating, lighting, drinking water, clean toilets and adequate maintenance. Accessibility must be treated as a basic requirement, not as an afterthought. At the same time, Srinagar should avoid replacing natural landscapes with excessive concrete and imported ornamental designs. Native trees and plants are better suited to the valley’s climate and require less water and maintenance. The city’s planting policy should prioritise biodiversity, shade and ecological resilience. Mature trees, wherever possible, should be preserved rather than removed and replaced with saplings that may take decades to provide comparable benefits. Tree cutting for road widening or infrastructure projects should be governed by transparent rules. Authorities must publish tree inventories, explain why removal is unavoidable and ensure that compensatory plantation is measurable and monitored. Planting a large number of saplings on paper cannot compensate for the loss of old trees if the saplings are poorly selected, unprotected or left to die. Accountability must extend beyond ceremonial plantation drives. The protection of green spaces cannot be left to government agencies alone. Residents’ associations, schools, colleges, civil society groups and local businesses should be involved in maintaining neighbourhood parks and reporting encroachments. But community participation must complement, not replace, state responsibility. Public spaces belong to the public, and the administration must provide the legal, financial and institutional support required to protect them. There is also a need to rethink the relationship between mobility and greenery. Roads should not be planned as mere channels for vehicles. Shaded footpaths, cycle routes, planted medians and green buffers can make movement safer and more comfortable. In many parts of Srinagar, walking is difficult because pavements are absent, broken or occupied. A city that wants to reduce congestion and pollution must make walking a practical choice. Green corridors can help connect neighbourhoods while improving public health. The restoration of urban waterways should form part of the same effort. Drains, streams and natural channels are often treated as waste conduits, but they can become ecological and public assets if cleaned, protected and landscaped carefully. Such restoration would reduce flooding, improve local appearance and create continuous green networks across the city. The objective should not be cosmetic beautification alone. It should be the recovery of natural systems that help the city function. Srinagar’s policymakers must also recognise that climate change will intensify existing vulnerabilities. More erratic rainfall, warmer summers and pressure on water resources will demand resilient urban planning. Green spaces offer one of the most affordable and effective tools available. They cool neighbourhoods, absorb stormwater and reduce the burden on drainage and public health systems. Protecting them is not an indulgence reserved for affluent cities; it is a practical response to an uncertain future. The debate over urban development should not be framed as a choice between growth and greenery. The real choice is between planned growth and reckless expansion. A city can build housing, improve transport and create economic opportunities without sacrificing every open space. What it cannot do is continue treating nature as an obstacle to development and expect the urban environment to remain liveable. Srinagar deserves a development model that respects its geography rather than overriding it. Its lakes, wetlands, gardens, trees and open spaces should be regarded as assets that support the economy and public well-being, not as land banks awaiting conversion. A city’s strength is not measured only by the number of buildings it adds, but also by the quality of air its residents breathe, the shade available on its streets, the water it can absorb and the spaces where its people can gather freely. The disappearance of green spaces is often gradual, almost invisible in the beginning. One tree is cut, one field is fenced, one wetland is filled, one park is neglected. By the time the cumulative loss becomes obvious, restoration becomes difficult and expensive. Srinagar still has an opportunity to change course. But that opportunity will not remain open indefinitely. Urban green spaces are not empty spaces. They are the city’s lungs, memory and protection. To save them is to defend Srinagar’s future. (The author is a freelance writer and environmental activist)

stories.headline: JKERA told to explore new funding sources
stories.title: JKERA told to explore new funding sources
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: Secretary, Planning, Development and Monitoring Department, Dr Owais Ahmad, on Monday directed the J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency (JKERA) to prepare a sustainable, Union Territory-wide infrastructure roadmap with a pipeline of innovative, fund-ready projects and proactively explore funding through Central schemes and other agencies to accelerate development across Jammu and Kashmir. Chairing a meeting to review the agency’s overall functioning, Dr Owais stressed the need to identify viable projects and mobilise additional resources to strengthen infrastructure development across key sectors in the Union Territory. Chief Executive Officer JKERA Akriti Sagar informed that since its creation in 2004 the J&KERA has played a pivotal role in up gradation of basic infrastructure in the Union Territory of J&K. She apprised that the agency has successfully implemented three major Externally Aided Projects (EAPs) across Jammu and Kashmir. These included the Multisector Project for Infrastructure Rehabilitation in J&K (MPIR) and the Jammu and Kashmir Urban Sector Development Investment Programme (JKUSDIP), both funded by the Asian Development Bank, besides the World Bank-funded Jhelum Tawi Flood Recovery Project (JTFRP). She added that major areas of intervention by J&KERA included basic infrastructure and critical infrastructure in health, education, livelihood and strengthening of disaster management. These included construction of state-of-the-art infrastructure in urban transportation - flyovers and grade separators, mega storm water drainage projects, construction of rural roads and bridges, buildings in health, higher education and school education sectors, livelihood initiatives, disaster management and urban reforms like water metering and capacity building of urban local bodies. stories.headline: Mohra hydel capacity reduced amid water shortage
stories.title: Mohra hydel capacity reduced amid water shortage
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 19: The Jammu and Kashmir government has reduced the capacity of the 125-year-old Mohra Hydroelectric Power Project in north Kashmir’s Uri area from 9 megawatts (MW) to 6 MW due to limited water availability, even as the restoration plan for the historic project has been finalised. Rahul Yadav, Managing Director of the Jammu and Kashmir State Power Development Corporation (JKSPDC), told Rising Kashmir that the Detailed Project Report (DPR) prepared by IIT Roorkee was ready and the corporation was awaiting approval from higher authorities to initiate the tendering process. “The capacity has been reduced because of the limited water available to us. Currently, the water of the Jhelum is being utilised by NHPC’s ongoing Uri-I stage-II project, while we will be using water from Boniyar nallah for the Mohra power project,” Yadav said. He said the heritage project would be restored under the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) model. “The final DPR for its restoration has been prepared by IIT Roorkee. We are awaiting government approval so that the tendering process can begin,” he said. The latest development marks a significant step towards reviving one of Kashmir’s oldest hydropower installations, which has remained defunct since the devastating floods of 1992. The government has renewed efforts to renovate, modernise and upgrade the project, with the JKSPDC Board of Directors earlier deciding to engage a transaction adviser to take the restoration process forward. In May this year, a team from IIT Roorkee visited the project site in Uri following suggestions for changes to its design. The updated DPR was intended to establish the technical requirements, estimated costs and implementation framework for the restoration. The project had earlier been considered under the Prime Minister’s Development Package for small hydropower development. In a reply to the Assembly in March 2025, the government had said IIT Roorkee, following a feasibility assessment conducted through the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), had recommended a 10.5 MW project for central financial assistance. The estimated project cost was Rs 135.02 crore at 2022 price levels, while the proposal for financial assistance was under appraisal with the Centre, the government had informed the House. Commissioned in 1905, the Mohra Hydroelectric Project played a pioneering role in bringing electricity to Srinagar when hydropower generation was still in its early stages in the region. One of its distinctive engineering features was an approximately 11-kilometre-long wooden flume that carried water from the upper reaches to the powerhouse to drive its turbines. The water-conductor system reflected the engineering challenges of the mountainous terrain and also served local irrigation needs. The project initially had an installed capacity of around 4 MW, which was subsequently enhanced. A 9 MW powerhouse was commissioned in 1962, while the project’s capacity was later reported at 10.5 MW. However, the devastating floods of 1992 severely damaged its infrastructure, eventually bringing power generation to a halt. For residents of Uri, the proposed restoration carries significance beyond electricity generation. The revival could help preserve a landmark of Kashmir’s industrial and technological history while opening up opportunities for heritage tourism and local employment.
